file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: are in the untwisted sector for the dual 1-form symmetry.From the discussion in section 3.4.1, we see that this is the SO(3)−theory. 4.3.5 Gauging Exchanges Mixed ’t Hooft Anomalies and Group Extensions Consider gauging a proper subgroup H(p) ⊆G(p) , (4.189) of a p-form symmetry group G(p).The gauged theory contains not only a dual H(d−p−2) = bH(p) , (4.190) (d −p −2)-form symmetry, but also a residual K(p) := G(p)/H(p) , (4.191) p-form symmetry.Depending on how H(p) is embedded inside G(p), the two symmetries of the gauged theory carry a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: In order to see this, note that a background field BG p+1 for G(p) p-form symmetry decom- poses as BG p+1 = i(BH p+1) + eBK p+1 , (4.192) where BH p+1 and BK p+1 are background fields for H(p) and K(p) respectively in the ungauged theory, i is the injective homomorphism i : H(p) →G(p) , (4.193) and eBK p+1 is a lift to G(p) of the K(p)-valued field BK p+1.From the analogous discussion around (4.107), we see that the above relationship implies δBH p+1 = −Bock(BK p+1) , (4.194) i.e.BH p+1 is not closed in general.After gauging H(p), the relation (4.194) becomes δbH p+1 = −Bock(BK p+1) , (4.195) for the gauge field bH p+1.The presence of coupling 2π Z Bd−p−1 ∪η bH p+1 , (4.196)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: where Bd−p−1 is background field for H(d−p−2) implies a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly in the gauged theory whose associated anomaly theory is Id+1 = exp  −2πis(d −p) Z Bd−p−1 ∪η Bock(BK p+1)  , s(d −p) = (−1)d−p .(4.197) Note that this anomaly vanishes if the short exact sequence 0 →H(p) →G(p) →K(p) →0 , (4.198) splits, as explained right before example (4.8).We are thus led to the following statement.Statement 4.6: Gauging Converts Group Extension to Mixed Anomaly Gauging a p-form symmetry group H(p) lying in an extension of p-form symmetry groups (4.198) leads to a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly of the form (4.197).The converse of the above statement is true, as can be seen by using the fact that gauging dual symmetry is equivalent to ungauging.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Statement 4.7: Gauging Converts Mixed Anomaly to Group Extension Gauging a (d −p −2)-form symmetry group having a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly with a p-form symmetry K(p) of the form (4.197) leads to a dual p-form symmetry H(p) which combines with the residual K(p) symmetry to form an extended G(p) p-form symmetry, such that the three p-form symmetries are related via (4.198).Example 4.16: Spin(6) vs.SO(6) pure Yang-Mills The mixed ’t Hooft anomaly (4.136) in pure SO(6) Yang-Mills theory can be seen as an example of statement (4.6) as the SO(6) theory is obtained by gauging Z2 subgroup of the Z4 electric 1-form symmetry of the pure Spin(6) Yang-Mills theory.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The non-triviality of the anomaly is related to the fact that the short exact sequence 0 →Z2 →Z4 →Z2 →0 , (4.199) does not split. 4.4 Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking and Confinement 4.4.1 General Concepts Just like ordinary 0-form global symmetries, higher p-form global symmetries can also ex- hibit spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB).We will see that spontaneous breaking is closely related to confinement.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: SSB of 0-Form Symmetries.Let us begin by rephrasing spontaneous symmetry break- ing of 0-form symmetries in a form that generalizes to p-form symmetries.The traditional definition is as follows.Definition 4.8: Spontaneous Breaking of 0-Form Symmetry A 0-form symmetry group G(0) is spontaneously broken if there exists a local operator O satisfying the following two conditions: 1.O is charged non-trivially under G(0), 2.The vev of O is non-zero ⟨O⟩̸ = 0 .(4.200) The main requirement (4.200) can be equivalently stated in terms of the non-vanishing of an asymptotic two point correlation function of O lim |x−y|→∞⟨O(x)O(y)⟩= ⟨O(x)⟩⟨O(y)⟩= ⟨O⟩⟨O⟩̸ = 0 , (4.201) where we have used cluster decomposition to convert a two point correlator at large distances into a product of one point correlators.SSB of p-Form Symmetries.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Generalizing (4.201), the spontaneous breaking of a p-form symmetry is defined as follows.Definition 4.9: Spontaneous Breaking of p-Form Symmetry A p-form symmetry group G(p) is spontaneously broken if there is a p-dimensional oper- ator Op charged non-trivially under G(p) having asymptotic correlation function lim R→∞⟨Op(Sp R)⟩̸ = 0 , (4.202) where Op is inserted along Sp R, which is a p-dimensional sphere of radius R.Note that for p = 0, this matches (4.201), as a 0-dimensional sphere consists of two points.Relationship to Confinement.Such an operator Op satisfying (4.202) survives in the deep IR.On the other hand, if an operator O′ p satisfies lim R→∞ D O′ p(Sp R) E = 0 , (4.203) then the operator Op does not exist in the IR.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Consequently, one says that an operator O′ p satisfying (4.203) confines in the IR, whereas operator Op satisfying (4.202) deconfines in the IR.Thus, we have the following statement Statement 4.8: (De)Confinement and SSB If a p-dimensional operator charged under a p-form symmetry G(p) deconfines, then G(p) is spontaneously broken.On the other hand, if all charged p-dimensional operators confine, then G(p) is not broken spontaneously.Relationship to Perimeter and Area Laws.Another well-known definition of confine- ment and deconfinement, in the context of line operators, is as follows: • If the asymptotic vev of a line operator L behaves as lim R→∞⟨L(S1 R)⟩∼exp (−αR) , (4.204) the line L is said to exhibit perimeter law.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: In such a situation, L deconfines. • On the other hand, if the asymptotic vev of a line operator L behaves as lim R→∞⟨L(S1 R)⟩∼exp  −αR2 , (4.205) the line L is said to exhibit area law.In such a situation, L confines.Naively, both perimeter and area laws seem to satisfy the condition (4.203) for confinement.However, the crucial point is that we can modify a line operator L satisfying perimeter law (4.204) by a counterterm localized along the line to obtain a new line operator L′ L′(S1 R) := L(S1 R) × exp Z S1 R vol !, (4.206) where vol is the volume form on S1 R.The operator L′ now exhibits (4.202) and hence decon- fines.One then says that the original line L deconfines, keeping the above understanding in mind.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: On the other hand, one cannot add a similar local counterterm to a line operator L satis- fying area law (4.205): • If one adds a counterterm localized along the line, then the resulting line operator L′ still confines.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: R T L Figure 20: A line operator L inserted along a rectangle in spacetime, with length R along a spatial direction and length T along time direction. • If one wants a deconfining line L′, the counterterm needs to be defined along a surface Σ2 with boundary of Σ2 being the locus of the line operator L, e.g.L′(S1 R, Σ2) := L(S1 R) × exp Z Σ2 vol  , (4.207) where ∂Σ2 = S1 R and vol is the volume form on Σ2.However, in such a situation the resulting line operator L′ depends on Σ2, and hence is a non-genuine line operator attached to a surface operator.Potential Between Probe Particles.If we regard line operators as probe particles, the asymptotic vevs can be characterized in terms of potential energy between these probe parti- cles.For this, consider inserting a line operator L along a rectangle as shown in figure 20.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: This configuration can now be regarded as an amplitude in which two probe particles sit separated by a distance R for time interval T.The vev can then be evaluated as ⟨L⟩∼exp (−V (R)T) , (4.208) where V (R) is the potential energy between the probe particles.In such a characterization, the perimeter law corresponds to V (R) ∼constant , (4.209) and area law corresponds to V (R) ∼R .(4.210) Thus, for probe particles showing area law, it costs infinite energy to separate them infinitely far away from each other.In other words, the probe particles remain confined.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Note that the potential (4.210) for area law is as if the two particles are attached by a string for constant tension.This leads to the famous idea that confinement should be related to the existence of a dynamical string-like excitation, known as the confining string, such that the two probe particles live at its ends.Example 4.17: Meissner Effect The confining string is realized concretely in the context of Meissner effect in supercon- ductivity.The setup is that of a 4d U(1) gauge theory with a charged scalar ϕ.As we provide a non-zero vev to the scalar ⟨ϕ⟩̸ = 0 , (4.211) the Dirac string associated to a ’t Hooft line operator of magnetic charge m, which is a probe Dirac monopole, becomes a vortex string such that on a circle S1 = {0 ≤θ < 2π} , (4.212) around it we have ⟨ϕ⟩= veimθ .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (4.213) This is due to the fact that we have a holonomy I S1 A = m , (4.214) around the Dirac string.This vortex string acts as a confining string which confines the ’t Hooft operator.Coulomb Behavior.Consider a situation in which the IR effective theory is either a pure Maxwell theory or a pure non-abelian gauge theory.As is well-known, the potential between electric probe particles in such a theory falls with distance as V (R) ∼1 R .(4.215) Consequently a Wilson line W in such a theory deconfines.Magnetic probe particles also show Coulomb behavior, and hence we conclude that all dyonic line operators in such a theory deconfine.We are thus led to the following statements: Statement 4.9: SSB in Pure Maxwell Theory The electric 1-form and magnetic (d −3) form symmetries in pure Maxwell theory in d ≥4 are spontaneously broken.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Statement 4.10: SSB in Pure Yang-Mills Theory The electric 1-form and magnetic (d −3) form symmetries in a pure non-abelian gauge theory in d ≥5 are spontaneously broken.The restriction of spacetime dimension d in the above two statements arises because otherwise the beta function for the gauge coupling is negative and thus the gauge theory description is not a good effective description in the IR.See [178] for discussion of other interesting behaviors exhibited by line operators. 4.4.2 Example: 4d N = 1 SYM Theories with su(2) Gauge Algbebra Let us use the above concepts to discuss confinement and deconfinement in 4d N = 1 SU(2) and SO(3)± Super Yang-Mills (SYM) theories.Relationship to N = 2 SYM with Soft SUSY Breaking.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: These N = 1 SYM theories can be obtained as a limit µ →∞, (4.216) of the N = 1 gauge theories obtained by deforming pure N = 2 SU(2), SO(3)± SYM by an N = 1 preserving mass term µ Tr Φ2 , (4.217) where Φ is the N = 1 chiral multiplet sitting inside N = 2 vector multiplet.Conjecturally, the phase structure of N = 1 SYM theories is the same as the phase structure of N = 1 gauge theories at small values of µ.Dual Meissner Effect in Seiberg-Witten Theory.The phase structure of the softly deformed theory for small values of µ was determined by Seiberg and Witten in their landmark paper [77], where they exhibited an electric-magnetic dual version of Meissner effect leading to confinement of Wilson lines.Let us review this dual Meissner effect in more detail below.Vacua After N = 1 Deformation.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The N = 2 SYM theory has a moduli space of vacua, known as the Coulomb branch.The N = 1 deformation µ lifts all of these vacua except for two special points on the Coulomb branch, namely the monopole and dyon points, which survive as vacua of the N = 1 theory obtained after such a soft deformation.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: IR Effective Theory.In both vacua, the IR theory is similar to the one discussed in the superconductivity example above, namely a U(1) gauge theory with a scalar ϕ of gauge charge 1 that condenses ⟨ϕ⟩̸ = 0 .(4.218) Additionally, we have massive particle excitations of even magnetic charge.Confinement/Deconfinement of IR Line Operators.Now let us study the behavior exhibited by various line defects of the IR theory.First, note that the electrically charged condensate ⟨ϕ⟩completely screens the electric charge of probe particles.Hence the electric charge is irrelevant in the computation of asymptotic potential energy between probe particles.If the probe particles do not carry any magnetic charge, then one can separate them without any energy cost with potential (4.209), and hence all Wilson lines deconfine WIR n −→deconfine, n ∈Z .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (4.219) For probe particles with magnetic charges, we need to separate the analysis of even and odd magnetic charges.The presence of dynamical particles with even magnetic charge means that the vortex strings attached to probe Dirac monopoles of even magnetic charge can break with these dynamical particles providing new ends.Consequently such vortex strings are unable to generate an area law potential, and we learn that ’t Hooft lines of even magnetic charges deconfine HIR 2m −→deconfine, m ∈Z .(4.220) On the other hand, the ’t Hooft lines of odd magnetic charges confine as in the superconduc- tivity example HIR 2m+1 −→confine, m ∈Z .(4.221) In general, for dyonic lines we have DIR n,2m = WIR n HIR 2m −→deconfine, n, m ∈Z , DIR n,2m+1 = WIR n HIR 2m+1 −→confine, n, m ∈Z .(4.222) Identification Between UV and IR Line Operators.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: In order to apply the above confinement and deconfinement results to the original UV theory, we need to know the identi- fication between the UV and IR line operators, which was described in detail by Seiberg and Witten.The identification in both vacua involves an electric-magnetic duality, but the duality transformation is different in both vacua:

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: • Monopole Vacuum: In the monopole vacuum, the IR scalar ϕ carries a magnetic charge from the UV point of view, and thus one says that the N = 1 SU(2) theory exhibits monopole condensation in this vacuum.The map of line operators is −→HIR 2j , j ∈Z/2 , −→WIR n , n ∈Z , j,n ≡WUV −→DIR n,2j, j ∈Z/2, n ∈Z , (4.223) where HUV is a ’t Hooft operator whose associated cocharacter ϕ : U(1) →SO(3) , (4.224) has winding number n around a maximal torus U(1) ⊂SO(3) .(4.225) • Dyon Vacuum: In the dyon vacuum, the IR scalar ϕ carries a dyonic charge from the UV point of view, and thus one says that the N = 1 SU(2) theory exhibits dyon condensation in this vacuum.The map of line operators is −→HIR 2j , j ∈Z/2 , −→DIR n,−n, n ∈Z , j,n ≡WUV −→DIR n,2j−n, j ∈Z/2, n ∈Z .(4.226) Confinement/Deconfinement of UV Line Operators.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Using the above maps (4.223), (4.226) and the behavior (4.222) of IR lines, we can now deduce the behavior exhibited by UV lines: • Monopole Vacuum: In the monopole vacuum, the UV lines exhibit the following behaviors: −→confine, j̸ ∈Z , −→deconfine, j ∈Z , −→deconfine, n ∈Z , j,n −→confine, j̸ ∈Z, n ∈Z , j,n −→deconfine, j ∈Z, n ∈Z .(4.227)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: • Dyon Vacuum: In the dyon vacuum, the UV lines exhibit the following behaviors: WUV j −→confine, j̸ ∈Z , WUV j −→deconfine, j ∈Z , HUV n −→deconfine, n ∈2Z , HUV n −→confine, n̸ ∈2Z , j,n −→deconfine, 2j −n ∈2Z , j,n −→confine, 2j −n̸ ∈2Z .(4.228) SU(2) Theory.Let us now pick gauge group G = SU(2) , (4.229) for the UV gauge theory, and study what happens in the IR.The charged genuine line operators are j,n , j̸ ∈Z, n ∈2Z , (4.230) which confine in both vacua.Thus, we learn the following.Statement 4.11: 1-Form SSB in 4d N = 1 SU(2) SYM The Z2 1-form symmetry of 4d N = 1 SU(2) SYM theory is spontaneously unbroken in both vacua.The IR theory in both vacua should be a 4d TQFT with Z2 1-form symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: To determine this TQFT, we need to study the operators surviving in the IR: • Monopole Vacuum: We need to take into account line operators j,n , j ∈Z, n ∈Z , (4.231) and the surface operator U2 , (4.232) generating the Z2 1-form symmetry.The genuine line operators are for n ∈2Z, which are all uncharged under the 1-form symmetry.This implies that the 1-form symmetry must be non-faithful in the IR, i.e.U2 must be isomorphic to the identity surface operator in the IR.This follows from the fact that any non-identity genuine topological operator in a TQFT has to braid non-trivially with some other non-identity genuine topological operator of the TQFT.Since U2 does not braid non-trivially with any of the lines, it

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: must be the identity operator.This implies that all line operators in (4.231) are genuine lines, but there is no non-identity surface operator available for them to braid with.Consequently, all the IR line operators must be identity as well.Thus, we obtain a completely trivial theory in the IR which carries only identity operators.So far we have not included the coupling of Z2 1-form symmetry in the IR theory.There are two possibilities because of the existence of a non-trivial SPT phase (4.161) for Z2 1-form symmetry in 4d.In order to determine this, we need to choose a coupling for the Z2 1-form symmetry in the UV, which is a choice of whether the non-trivially charged lines in the twisted sector are DUV j,n , j̸ ∈Z, n̸ ∈2Z , (4.233) or DUV j,n , j ∈Z, n̸ ∈2Z .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (4.234) Conventionally, the choice (4.233) is known simply as the SU(2) theory, while the choice (4.234) is known as the TSU(2) theory.For the SU(2) theory, none of the charged lines survive in the IR and hence we obtain trivial SPT phase.On the other hand, for TSU(2) theory, we do have charged lines in the twisted sector in IR, and hence we obtain the non-trivial SPT phase.Thus the IR 4d TQFTs with Z2 1-form symmetry are TM SU(2) = Trivial , TM TSU(2) = SPT , (4.235) where SPT denotes the non-trivial SPT phase and the superscript M denotes the monopole vacuum. • Dyon Vacuum: The line operators that need to be taken into account are DUV j,n −→deconfine, 2j −n ∈2Z .(4.236) The genuine line operators have j ∈Z, n ∈2Z which are uncharged under 1-form symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Thus U2 must again be identity operator and similar to the case for monopole vacuum all line operators must also be identity.The IR theory is thus trivial if one does not take into account the Z2 1-form symmetry.Taking into account the Z2 1-form symmetry, the 4d TQFTs are TD SU(2) = SPT , TD TSU(2) = Trivial , (4.237) where the superscript D denotes the dyon vacuum.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Traditionally, the vacuum carrying trivial SPT is referred to as confining vacuum, while the non-trivial SPT is referred to as oblique confining vacuum.Note that the definition of SO(3)+ vs.TSO(3)+ theories is chosen such that gauging the Z2 1-form symmetry of the SU(2) theory leads to the SO(3)+ theory (as opposed to the TSO(3)+ theory).SO(3)+ Theory.Now pick the gauge group G = SO(3) , (4.238) with trivial discrete theta angle.The charged genuine line operators are DUV j,n , j ∈Z, n̸ ∈2Z , (4.239) which deconfine in the monopole vacuum, but confine in the dyon vacuum.Thus, we learn the following.Statement 4.12: 1-Form SSB in 4d N = 1 SO(3)+ SYM The Z2 1-form symmetry of 4d N = 1 SO(3)+ SYM theory is spontaneously broken in one vacuum and spontaneously unbroken in the other vacuum.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Let us study the IR TQFT in the two vacua. • Monopole Vacuum: Since we have charged genuine lines (4.239) that deconfine, U2 is a non-identity surface operator.Similarly all the lines (4.239) are non-identity topological operators.However, all these lines are the same in the IR.This is because if we had two different lines L1 and L2, then L−1 1 L2 would be a non-identity line that does not braid non-trivially with any surface, leading to a contradiction.Let us denote this IR line operator as U1.Thus we have an emergent 2-form symmetry in the IR as a consequence of deconfinement!We can recognize the properties of U2 and U1 as that of surface and line operators in a 4d Z2 gauge theory π Z a1 ∪δb2 , (4.240) which is the IR effective theory TM SO(3)+ = Z2 Gauge Theory .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (4.241) We can modify the 1-form coupling in the UV and begin with TSO(3)+ theory, but this only impacts twisted sector lines, which all confine, and hence the coupling does not impact the IR physics TM TSO(3)+ = Z2 Gauge Theory .(4.242)

text: • Dyon Vacuum: The story here is similar to the SU(2) cases discussed above, and one finds that SO(3)+ = SPT , TSO(3)+ = Trivial , (4.243) where the 1-form coupling for SO(3)+ is chosen such that the charged twisted sector lines are Dj,n, j̸ ∈Z, n̸ ∈2Z , (4.244) and for TSO(3)+ the charged twisted sector lines are Dj,n, j̸ ∈Z, n ∈2Z .(4.245) SO(3)−Theory.The analysis is similar to the SO(3)+ case and is left to the interested reader.The final results are TM SO(3)−= SPT , TM TSO(3)−= Trivial , SO(3)−= Z2 Gauge Theory , TSO(3)−= Z2 Gauge Theory .(4.246) Note that the definition of SO(3)−vs.TSO(3)−theories is chosen such that gauging the Z2 1-form symmetry of the TSU(2) theory leads to the SO(3)−theory (as opposed to the TSO(3)−theory).

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Confining Non-Lagrangian Theories In the above study of confinement/deconfinement in 4d N = 1 SYM, the Lagrangian descriptions were crucial for obtaining the presented results.However, the definitions of confinement and deconfinement do not require any Lagrangian description.This raises the question of how to study confinement/deconfinement in non-Lagrangian or strongly coupled 4d theories.An answer to this question was provided recently in [68] for theories that admit a construction in terms of M5 branes in M-theory, or as compactifications of 6d N = (2, 0) SCFTs, where examples of confining non-Lagrangian theories are also provided.S and T Operations.All the UV theories considered above are related by gaugings.We have already discussed two such gaugings SU(2)/Z(1) = SO(3)+ , TSU(2)/Z(1) = SO(3)−.(4.247)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: It is customary to denote the gauging by S.In terms of this, the above gaugings are represented as relations S(SU(2)) = SO(3)+ , ST(SU(2)) = SO(3)−.(4.248) Thus, S is the operation of gauging, and T is the operation of stacking an SPT phase.It can be shown [4,93] that these operations obey (ST)3 = 1 , (4.249) which is an identity also satisfied by the S and T matrices generating the SL(2, Z) group.For this reason, the above and S and T operations are referred to as “SL(2, Z) operations on 4d QFTs with Z2 1-form symmetry”.It should be noted that T is an order two operation in our context, rather than the usual infinite order operation.Combining it with the fact that gauging twice is the same as ungauging, i.e.S2 = 1 .(4.250) we find that the group of these S and T transformations is PSL(2, Z2).

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The full web of gaugings can be deduced by using the relationship (4.249) along with (4.247).For example, if one wants to know the result of gauging the Z2 1-form symmetry of the TSO(3)−theory, one is computing S(TSO(3)−) = STST(SU(2)) = TS(SU(2)) = TSO(3)+ .(4.251) Alternatively, one can use the exchange of charged and twisted sectors of line operators under 1-form gauging to deduce the theory after gauging.Compatibility Between UV and IR Gaugings.One can also consider gauging 1-form symmetries of the IR TQFTs discussed above.We have S(Trivial) = Z2 Gauge Theory , S(SPT) = SPT , S(Z2 Gauge Theory) = Trivial .(4.252) This can be easily seen by exchanging the twisted and charged sectors of line operators: • In the trivial theory, we have a twisted sector line that is uncharged.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: This is simply the identity line living at the end of U2, which as we discussed is simply the identity surface operator.After gauging, this line gives rise to a charged line in the untwisted sector, which means that the gauged theory is the Z2 gauge theory.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: • In the SPT theory, we have a twisted sector line that is charged.After gauging, it remains in the twisted sector and also remains charged.Thus, the gauged theory is SPT again. • In the Z2 gauge theory, we have an untwisted sector line that is charged.After gauging, it becomes a line in the twisted sector that is uncharged.Thus, the gauged theory is the trivial theory.The T operations are T(Trivial) = SPT , T(SPT) = Trivial , T(Z2 Gauge Theory) = Z2 Gauge Theory .(4.253) Now S and T transformations should commute with the RG flow.Indeed, this can be explicitly checked.For example, we should have S  TM SU(2)  = TM S(SU(2)) = TM SO(3)+ , (4.254) which is indeed the case.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: As another example, we should have S  TD TSO(3)−  = TD TSO(3)+ , (4.255) which the reader can easily see is also true. 4.5 Symmetry TFTs We have seen that any gauging of discrete symmetries can be ungauged, simply by a subsequent gauging of the dual symmetry.This means that discrete gaugings do not change the full information of observables in a theory.However, as we have seen, discrete gaugings do mix different types of observables into each other, e.g. the exchange of twisted and charged sectors discussed in section 4.3.4.As a consequence, a physical observable may appear in different contexts in different gauge frames associated to a discrete symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Symmetry topological field theories (TFTs), abbreviated SymTFTs or Symmetry TFTs, are powerful tools that detangle the physical observables from their behavior in different gauge frames.They also encode the ’t Hooft anomalies of the symmetry and possible higher-group structures.We refer the reader to [179] for general logic of SymTFTs, and to [4,102,180] for detailed discussions of SymTFTs in the context of invertible symmetries.Recently, detailed discussions of SymTFTs for non-invertible symmetries appeared in [60], which also elucidated the general concepts of [179].

text: Bphys Bsym Z(S) Figure 21: The sandwich construction as explained in the text.We have also displayed topo- logical operators and their junctions generating symmetry S as a Y-shape.These operators are localized on the symmetry boundary Bsym .Sandwich Construction.The basic idea of SymTFT is encoded in the sandwich construc- tion.Let us first present the idea abstractly, and then we will concretely illustrate it.Consider a d-dimensional theory T with some discrete symmetry S.This could be a higher-form or a higher-group (or even a non-invertible) symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: According to the sand- wich construction, we can realize T as an interval compactification involving the following ingredients: • Symmetry TFT: This is a (d + 1)-dimensional TQFT Z(S) associated only to the symmetry S and independent of the theory T. • Symmetry Boundary Condition: This is a topological boundary condition Bsym of the SymTFT Z(S) which also only depends on the symmetry S and independent of the theory T. • Physical Boundary Condition: This is a possibly non-topological boundary condition Bphys of the SymTFT Z(S) which is different for different theories T.See figure 21.The symmetry S is separated onto the symmetry boundary Bsym , while the dynamics of the theory T lives on the boundary Bphys .SymTFTs for Higher-Form Symmetries.Let the symmetry S be a product of discrete higher-form symmetries S = n Y i=1 G(pi) , (4.256)

text: Bphys T Z(S) T S Gauging S in (d + 1)-dimensions Figure 22: The SymTFT Z(S) and physical boundary Bphys T for a d-dimensional theory T having invertible symmetry S are constructed by gauging S in (d + 1)-dimensions. with a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly captured by an anomaly theory Id+1[Ap1+1, Ap2+1, · · · , Apn+1] = exp  i Z Leff d+1[Ap1+1, Ap2+1, · · · , Apn+1]  , (4.257) where Api+1 are background fields for G(pi) symmetries and Leff d+1 is the effective Lagrangian for the anomaly theory.We assume that any 0-form symmetries appearing in S are abelian.For non-abelian 0-form symmetries, we need a generalization of what is discussed here.See [60] for more details.Then the right half of the sandwich construction involving the SymTFT and the physical boundary is obtained by gauging all the G(pi) symmetries.

text: Note that this is impossible in d-dimensions unless the ’t Hooft anomaly vanishes, but here we are performing the gauging in (d + 1)-dimensions, which is possible after attaching SPT phase Id+1 to the theory T.See figure 22.As an SPT phase is a trivial theory once we forget about the symmetry, the gauging procedure leads to a discrete higher-form gauge theory, but this theory generally is not of the type discussed in section 2.3.The presence of the SPT phase modifies the action of the gauge theory to n X i=1 2π Z api+1 ∪η δbd−pi−1 + Z Leff d+1[ap1+1, ap2+1, · · · , apn+1] .(4.258) Now, to complete the sandwich construction, we need to provide the symmetry boundary condition.This is comprised of • Dirichlet boundary condition (b.c.) for all gauge fields api+1. • Neumann b.c. for all gauge fields bd−pi−1.

text: Example 4.18: Gauging a Higher-Form Symmetry Consider a theory T carrying a non-anomalous discrete p-form symmetry G(p) (for p = 0 we only consider abelian G(0)).As we discussed above, the action for the SymTFT is 2π Z ap+1 ∪η δbd−p−1 .(4.261) Let us choose a topological boundary condition Bsym • Neumann boundary condition (b.c.) for gauge field ap+1. • Dirichlet b.c. for gauge field bd−p−1.The sandwich construction now constructs the theory T′ = T/G(p) .(4.262) Indeed, the topological operators on Bsym are Ubg which generate G(d−p−2) = bG(p) , (4.263)

text: Let us see this explicitly in an example: Example 4.19: Pure SO(6) Yang-Mills theory Recall from example 4.8 that pure SO(6) gauge theory has a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly between G(1) = Ze 2 electric 1-form symmetry and G(d−3) = Zm 2 (d −3)-form symmetry given by Id+1[Ae 2, Am d−2] = exp  πi Z Am d−2 ∪Bock(Ae 2)  .(4.265) The SymTFT has action π Z �ae 2 ∪δbe d−2 + am d−2 ∪δbm 2 + am d−2 ∪Bock(ae 2)  .(4.266) The equation of motion descending from am d−2 is δbm 2 = Bock(ae 2) , (4.267) which means that imposing Dirichlet b.c. on bm 2 requires imposing Dirichlet b.c. on ae 2.In other words, we cannot impose Dirichlet b.c. on both bm 2 and be d−2 simultaneously, since the latter Dirichlet b.c. implies Neumann b.c. for ae 2.

text: Said differently, we cannot gauge both the electric and magnetic higher-form symmetries simultaneously, which is also the obstruction imposed by the ’t Hooft anomaly (4.265).Higher-Group Symmetries Higher group symmetries arise when higher-form symmetries of different degrees mix with each other.This means that performing a gauge transformation of background field Bp+1

text: for a p-form symmetry shifts also the background field Bq+1 for a q-form symmetry.If r is the largest integer for which an r-form symmetry participates in the higher-group, then the higher-group is an (r + 1)-group.We will focus mainly on simplest types of higher-groups, namely 2-group symmetries, which involve only 0-form and 1-form symmetries.A lot of work has been performed on this subject.The foundational papers discussing higher-group symmetries in QFT are [181–184].The discussion of higher-group symmetries in strongly coupled QFTs via string theory and compactifications of higher-dimensional QFTs began in [185–187].See [188–206] for a sample of other works (in no particular order) on higher-group symmetries. 5.1 Continuous Higher-Group Symmetries Example: Gauging Mixed ’t Hooft Anomaly.

text: Let us begin with an example of a higher- group symmetry in which the constituent p-form symmetry groups are all continuous [183].Gauged versions of such continuous higher-groups are famously encountered in the Green- Schwarz mechanism of anomaly cancellation.Let us begin with a d-dimensional theory having a p-form symmetry U(1)(p) and a (d − 2p −4)-form symmetry U(1)(d−2p−4) with a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly W[Bp+1+dΛp, Bd−2p−3+dΛd−2p−4] = W[Bp+1, Bd−2p−3]+2πκ Z Λp∧Hp+2∧Hd−2p−2 .(5.1) Here κ ∈Z characterizes the anomaly, W is the effective action and Hp+2 and Hd−2p−2 are the field strengths of background fields Bp+1 and Bd−2p−3 respectively.Since there is no anomaly term dependent upon Λd−2p−4, we can gauge the U(1)(d−2p−4) symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: See the box below for more details. • p-branes wrapping compact k-cycles give rise to (p −k + 1)-dimensional dynamical ex- citations in the field theory T.These are classified by the homology group Hk(MD).Compactification of branes on non-compact cycles gives rise to defects because the mass of the compactified object in the effective QFT T is determined by the volume of the internal cycle, and infinitely massive objects can be regarded as defects.This is illustrated in figure 28. 7Until recently, research in this direction within the realm of string theory realizations of QFTs focused on identifying the string theory origin of the (not necessarily topological) charged defects under generalized symmetries.

text: With regards to the origin of the topological symmetry generators, [62,103] contained some early discussions in terms of flux operators.More recent works [136, 138, 139, 154] explain how, in an appropriate topological limit, wrapped branes in both geometric engineering and holographic constructions describe the topological symmetry generators.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Relative Homology By definition Hk(MD, ∂MD) is given by relative cycles modulo relative boundaries.The definition of a relative cycle relaxes that of an ordinary cycle: a relative chain x ∈Ck(MD) is a relative cycle if ∂x ∈Ck−1(∂MD).In relative homology, a relative cycle x is trivial if x = ∂y + z with y ∈Ck+1(MD) and z ∈Ck(∂MD).Screening and p-Form Symmetries.Accounting for screening of defects by dynamical excitations, we find that p-branes wrapping k-cycles in MD give rise to the following group of unscreened (p −k + 1)-dimensional operators Dp,k = Hk(MD, ∂MD;Z)/Hk(MD;Z) , (6.4) Combining all of these we obtain what is known as the defect group [62,63,201] D = M p,k Dp,k = M i Di , (6.5) where on the RHS we have reorganized D according to defects of dimension i.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: There is in general a non-degenerate pairing on D, which is a bi-homomorphism ⟨·, ·⟩: D × D →U(1) , (6.6) which captures mutual non-locality of the defects in D.The mutual non-locality captures the fact that not all of these defects can be simultaneously in the untwisted sector of the higher- form symmetries.Some of the defects have to be attached to topological operators generating the higher-form symmetries and non-locality arises as the defects pass these topological oper- ators and acquire phases according to their charges.There are various choices for consistently picking which defects will be twisted and which ones will be untwisted.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Each such choice corresponds to what is known as a polarization or a Lagrangian, which is Λ = M i Λi , (6.7) where each Λi is a subgroup Λi ⊆Di , (6.8) such that Λ is a maximal such subgroup on which the pairing trivializes ⟨·, ·⟩|Λ = 1 .(6.9)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: It should be noted though that not all such choices of Λ may be allowed due to the presence of ’t Hooft anomalies.Each allowed choice of Λ provides a ‘global form’ for the d-dimensional QFT being constructed.One can cycle between different global forms by performing discrete gaugings (possibly with discrete torsions) of the higher-form symmetries described below.Given an allowed Λ, the resulting d-dimensional QFT has higher-form symmetries SΛ = Y i G(i) , (6.10) such that the i-form symmetry group is G(i) = bΛi .(6.11) Consistency with Swampland Conjecture According to one of the swampland conjectures, a consistent theory of quantum gravity cannot have any global symmetries, including higher-form symmetries.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: In the context of geometric engineering, quantum gravity theories arise if the internal compactification manifold is compact, as then compactified theory carries a non-zero value of GN.All the higher-form symmetries that we discussed are associated to non-compact cycles in the internal manifold, and hence the swampland conjecture is satisfied here.More generally, see [208–214] for a sample of work at the interface of swampland and higher-form symmetries.Description in Terms of the Boundary.We can describe Dp−k+1 in terms of the bound- ary ∂MD of the internal manifold by using the long exact sequence in relative homology · · · →Hi(∂MD) hi −→Hi(MD) fi −→Hi(MD, ∂MD) gi −→Hi−1(∂MD) hi−1 −−−→Hi−1(MD) →. . . .(6.12) which implies Hk(MD, ∂MD)/Hk(MD) = im(gk) = ker(hk−1) , (6.13) and hence Dp,k = ker(hk−1) .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt

text: McKay correspondence.With a judicial choice of asymptotic fluxes [62,63], this configu- ration engineers pure 7d N = 1 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories with gauge algebra gADE.Let the corresponding simply connected group be denoted as GADE.From the gauge theory analysis discussed earlier, these theories have a defect group D = D1 ⊕D4 , (6.16) such that D1 ∼= D4 ∼= Z(GADE) , (6.17) where Z(GADE) is the center of GADE.Here D1 is the group of unscreened Wilson line operators and D4 is the group of unscreened ’t Hooft operators.Now let us compute the defect group using the geometric engineering analysis.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The boundary of internal manifold is ∂(C2/ΓADE) = S3/ΓADE , (6.18) whose first homology group is H1(S3/ΓADE) = Ab[ΓADE] = Z(GADE) , (6.19) where Ab[ΓADE] is the abelianization of the (generally non-abelian) group ΓADE, which is isomorphic to Z(GADE).All of these 1-cycles are contractible when pushed into the bulk.Thus wrapping M2 and M5 branes on them, we obtain the contributions D1 and D4 to (6.16).Description in Terms of Intersection Numbers.By Poincaré duality, we have8 Hk(MD, ∂MD) = HD−k(MD) , (6.20) where on the RHS we have homology group of compact (D−k)-cycles on the internal manifold MD.The relevant quotient can now be expressed as Dp,k = Hk(MD, ∂MD)/Hk(MD) = HD−k(MD)/Hk(MD) , (6.21) which requires an injective homomorphism i : Hk(MD) →HD−k(MD) .

text: (6.22) The map i maps a k-cycle Ck to a (D −k)-cycle i(Ck) = X j  Ck · Cj D−k  Cj D−k , (6.23) where Cj D−k is a basis of (D−k)-cycles in HD−k(MD) and Ck·Cj D−k is the intersection number between Ck and Cj D−k in MD. 8Here we are assuming that there is no torsion in homology of MD.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Example 6.2: 5d N = 1 SCFT: E1 Theory An interesting and well-known 5d N = 1 SCFT is the E1 theory whose characteristic property is that it flows to 5d N = 1 pure SU(2) gauge theory (with trivial discrete theta angle) after a mass deformation.This theory admits a geometric engineering construction in which the internal mani- fold is a non-compact Calabi-Yau threefold M6 containing a single compact 4-cycle which is topologically C4 = P1 × P1 .(6.24) The only compact 2-cycles are the two P1s inside C4, both of which have intersection number P1 · C4 = −2 .(6.25) Thus, we have for this geometry H2(M6, ∂M6)/H2(M6) = Z2 .(6.26) Wrapping M2 branes on these non-compact 2-cycles, we find a group D1 = Z2 , (6.27) of unscreened line operators.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: These line operators are in the untwisted sector in the E1 theory and thus we deduce a 1-form symmetry group G(1) = bD1 = Z2 .(6.28) for the E1 theory. 6.2 Generalised Symmetries in Holography In this subsection we will describe how generalised symmetries appear in holographic set- tings9.The content of this subsection is intimately linked to that of section 4.5 on Symmetry Topological Field Theory10.SymTFT from Holography.Consider a setup with background geometry AdSd+1 × XD−d−1 , (6.29) with D = 10, 11 and X representing some internal manifold11.

text: After dimensionally reducing 10/11d supergravity, and focusing on solely the dominant contributions at the boundary, one 9For early works see [95, 101], and for more recent applications see for example [99, 106, 133, 136, 138, 142, 161,175,177,194,215] 10See e.g. [175] for an in-depth discussion of the precise mapping between the SymTFT and the topological bulk terms in a holographic context. 11The restriction to AdS solutions here is just for illustration purposes.For example, the Klebanov-Strassler solution [216] is not of this type, but was studied using the below technology in [136,177,215]

text: is typically left with a bulk action of the form Sbulk = X p,i,j Z AdSd+1 Nij,p ai p+1 ∧dbj d−p−1 + A  {ai p+1}  , (6.30) where a, b are bulk gauge fields which are differential forms on spacetime of degrees determined by their subscript, Nij,p ∈Z and A is a function of gauge fields of type a.Let us assume that Nij,p define non-degenerate matrices for each p.Then Sbulk is a description of a discrete (higher-form) gauge theory of the form (4.258) in terms of continuous fields.And the claim is that Sbulk is the SymTFT associated to some (higher-form) symmetries of the holographically dual d-dimensional QFT.Symmetry Boundary Condition from Holography.As we discussed in section 4.5, various gauge frames or global forms of the d-dimensional QFT are obtained by choosing boundary conditions of the SymTFT gauge fields.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: In the holographic description, this corre- sponds to choosing boundary conditions for the gauge fields appearing in Sbulk along the AdS boundary.Let us discuss two examples: Example 6.3: AdS5 × S5: 4d N = 4 SYM Consider the famous AdS5 ×S5 setup in 10d IIB supergravity, which is dual to 4d N = 4 pure super Yang-Mills theories with gauge algebra su(N).Beginning with the 10d IIB supergravity solution, one expands the higher-form fields around the background solution.Plugging these fluctuations into the equations of motion and Bianchi identities of 10d supergravity produces a set of equations.Since we are interested in dominant boundary contributions, we truncate them to single derivative terms which are the leading terms at large distances.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: From this, one can reverse-engineer the topological action reproducing these equations of motion, and finds it to be [217] Stop = N Z AdS5 b2 ∧dc2 .(6.31) See [215] for more details on the procedure.Here b2, c2 are continuous bulk 2-form gauge fields which come from expanding the NSNS and RR 2-form gauge fields of IIB supergravity around the fixed background solution.The action Stop describes SymTFT for 1-form symmetries of N = 4 theories with su(N) gauge algebra.We now consider the possible choices of boundary conditions.(a) Boundary conditions 1.A simple choice of boundary conditions is b2 Dirichlet , c2 Neumann .(6.32)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The bulk equations of motion of the action (6.31) are Nb2 = 0 , Nc2 = 0 .(6.33) Compatibility with these equations of motion implies that these boundary conditions force c2 to vary within ZN in the boundary.Correspondingly Wilson surfaces for this ZN-valued gauge field on the boundary generate a 1-form symmetry, meaning that we have chosen a global form of the resulting 4d theory which carries a 1-form symmetry G(1) = ZN .(6.34) We claim that these boundary conditions correspond to choosing the global form which has gauge group G = SU(N) .(6.35) This can be seen holographically by considering the Bianchi identity for the 7-form flux, which sources D5-branes.In particular integrating over the compact space S5 we have S5 dF7 = S5 F5 ∧H3 = NH3 .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (6.36) This implies that N fundamental strings (which couple to b2) can be screened by ending on a D5-brane wrapped on S5, which is precisely the baryon vertex of [218].The fundamental strings become Wilson lines in the 4d gauge theory, and hence we learn that (6.34) is purely an electric 1-form symmetry, thus justifying (6.35).(b) Boundary conditions 2.Let us exchange the Neumann and Dirichlet properties of b2 and c2, now imposing the boundary conditions c2 Dirichlet , b2 Neumann .(6.37) By similar logic as above we learn that the 4d theory should have G(1) = ZN , (6.38) 1-form symmetry.However, this time the global form is G = PSU(N) , (6.39) gauge group with trivial discrete theta angle.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: This can again be justified holographically from the Bianchi identity for the other 7-form S5 dH7 = − S5 F5 ∧F5 = −NF3 , (6.40) which implies that N D1 strings (which couple to c2) can be screened by ending on an NS5-brane wrapped on S5.Since the D1 strings become ’t Hooft lines in the 4d gauge theory, we learn that (6.38) is purely a magnetic 1-form symmetry, thus justifying (6.39).

text: (c) More general boundary conditions.More general boundary conditions give rise to other possible global forms for the gauge group and possible discrete theta angles.See [215] for a discussion of some of these.Example 6.4: AdS4 × S7/Zk: 3d ABJM Theories The low-energy description of a stack of N M2-branes probing a C4/Zk singularity is a three-dimensional Chern-Simons matter gauge theory with gauge group U(N)k×U(N)−k [219].The large N holographic dual is 11d supergravity on AdS4 × S7/Zk.There are many possible global variants [220,221] U(N)k × U(N)−k , SU(N)k × SU(N)−k , (SU(N)k × SU(N)−k) /ZN (U(N)k × U(N)−k) /Zm′ , (SU(N)k × SU(N)−k) /Zn′ , (6.41) where m′ is a divisor of k and n′ a divisor of N.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: In [95] the authors give a holographic origin for all these variants using the type of analysis discussed above, where they used 10d IIA supergravity.They argue that the 4d SymTFT contains a BF term S4d = Z M4 B2 ∧(NdAD0 + kdAD4) .(6.42) Here B2 is the NS-NS 2-form gauge field and the A fields are 1-form gauge fields sourced by D0 and D4 branes respectively.We explain how to derive this term using IIA supergravity below.Applying different boundary conditions to the BF term gives a suite of 3d theories with different global symmetries and global gauge groups.Let us now derive the topological action (6.42) from the equations of motion of 10- dimensional type IIA supergravity.The AdS4 × S7/Zk M-theory has a description in Type IIA string theory on AdS4 × CP 3.The background fluxes are as follows Z CP 3 F6 2π ∼N , Z CP1⊂CP 3 F2 2π ∼k .

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (6.43) We will follow the general philosophy outlined in [215] to derive an effective topological action in four dimensions.We first expand the form fields of Type IIA on the cohomology of the internal space, making a choice of dualization frame (i.e. expanding F2 or F8 etc.).The internal space CP 3 has homology H0(CP 3;Z) = H2(CP 3;Z) = H4(CP 3;Z) = H6(CP 3;Z) = Z , H1(CP 3;Z) = H3(CP 3;Z) = H5(CP 3;Z) = 0 .(6.44) We choose to represent H2, H4 by forms ω2, ω4, and normalise such that ω2 ∧ω4 = volCP 3 .(6.45)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Furthermore, we choose to expand in F2 and F6, for which we have explicit flux quanti- sation conditions without needing to resort to the Hodge dual operation F2 = kω2 + g2 , F6 = Nω2 ∧ω4 + f2 ∧ω4 + f4 ∧w2 , H3 = h3 + h1 ∧w2 .(6.46) F4, F8 are obtained via the relations F4 = ∗F6, F8 = ∗F2: F4 = NvolAdS4 + ∗4f2 ∧ω2 + ∗4f4 ∧ω4 , F8 = kvolAdS4 ∧ω4 + ∗4g2 ∧ω2 ∧ω4 , (6.47) where we have used the identity ∗6ω2 = ω4 and ∗10volAdS4 = ω2 ∧ω4.We now plug these expansions into the Type IIA equations of motion and Bianchi identities.We wish to identify leading order topological contributions: we immediately drop terms that are not topological or have more than one derivative.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-05_广义对称性讲义/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Cycling through the various equations of motion we obtain d ∗10 F2 = H3 ∧F6 0 = Nh3 ∧ω2 ∧ω4 , (6.48) and d ∗10 H3 = F2 ∧F6 0 = (kf2 + Ng2) ∧ω2 ∧ω4 , (6.49) and d ∗10 F6 = H3 ∧F2 0 = kh3 ∧ω2 .(6.50) From the Bianchi identities, dF6 = H3 ∧F4, dF2 = H3 ∧F0, dH3 = 0, we isolate the following relevant contributions (setting F0 = 0) df2 = 0 , dh3 = 0 , dg2 = 0 , (6.51) such that we can define gauge fields a1, b2, c1 f2 = da1 , h3 = db2 , g2 = dc1 .(6.52) We are therefore left with three topological, single derivative contributions Ndb2 = 0 , kdb2 = 0 , kda1 + Ndc1 = 0 , (6.53) which are exactly the equations of motion of (6.42) with the following identifications b2 ↔B2 , c1 ↔AD0 , a1 ↔AD4 .(6.54)

text: IPMU-16-0048 A brief review of the 2d/4d correspondences Yuji Tachikawa Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe, University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8583, Japan [邮箱隐去] Abstract An elementary introduction to the 2d/4d correspondences is given.After quickly reviewing the 2d q-deformed Yang-Mills theory and the Liouville theory, we will introduce 4d theories obtained by coupling trifundamentals to SU(2) gauge ﬁelds.We will then see concretely that the supersymmetric partition function of these theories on S3 × S1 and on S4 is given respectively by the q-deformed Yang-Mills theory and the Liouville theory.After giving a short discussion on how this correspondence may be understood from the viewpoint of the 6d N = (2, 0) theory, we conclude the review by enumerating future directions.

text: Introduction The aim of this review article is to give an elementary account of the 2d/4d correspondence, originally found in [2,3].Let us begin by presenting the essential idea, which is in fact quite simple.We start from a certain six-dimensional quantum ﬁeld theory S, and consider its partition function on a product manifold X4 × C2, where X4 is four-dimensional and C2 is two- dimensional.Let us further suppose that thanks to the supersymmetric twists, the resulting partition function depends on the shapes but not on the sizes of X4 and C2.Then the six- dimensional partition function S(X4 × C2) can be evaluated in two ways.On the one hand, if we make C2 very small, we ﬁrst have a four-dimensional theory S(C2), and then we can consider its partition function on X4, namely S(C2)(X4).On the other hand, if we make

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: X4 very small, we ﬁrst have a two-dimensional theory S(X4), and then we can consider its partition function on C2, namely S(X4)(C2).We now have an equality S(X4)(C2) = S(C2)(X4).(1.1) So far the construction is extremely general.To get something concrete, we need to make a choice.As an example, let us take S to be the 6d N=(2, 0) theory of type A1, and C2 to be an arbitrary two-dimensional surface.The 4d theory S(C2) thus obtained is often called a class S theory of type A1, and is an N=2 supersymmetric theory with a number of SU(2) gauge group factors coupled to a number of trifundamental ﬁelds [4].If we choose X4 = S4, the partition function S(C2)(X4) can be computable by localization [5,6], and from the results of the computation, one sees that S(S4) is the Liouville theory, which is a non-compact 2d conformal ﬁeld theory [2].

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: If we choose X4 = S3 × S1, the partition function S(C2)(X4) is called the superconformal index [7,8], and from the results of the computation, one sees that S(S3×S1) is the q-deformed SU(2) Yang-Mills theory [3,9].These are the simplest cases of the correspondences, and various generalizations are possible and have been carried out.It is already ﬁve years since these correspondences were originally found1, and countless pages of original articles have been already wasted to describe the details and the general- izations.The number of the review articles devoted to this topic is also already quite large.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: However, this huge amount of information can also be somewhat daunting, and the author therefore feels that it would be not completely useless to have another concise review, so that a newly interested reader can quickly go through to have an idea of how this correspondence came to be known, where the details can be learned, and what are still unsolved problems s/he might want to study.This article is therefore intentionally meant to be a shallow overview.Many of the facts will be stated as facts and will not be explained.Details and subtleties will be mentioned but will not be treated in full;references to review or original articles will be given instead.2 The presentation will not be completely logical either.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: It would be most systematic to start from six dimensions, to analyze the compactiﬁcation very carefully, and to arrive at the correspondence at the last step.Thanks to the recent developments, it would not be impossible to write a review in this order.This will, however, be a hard read for people new to this ﬁeld.Instead, this review will be organized to explain how the correspondence works instead of why there is the correspondence.In Sec. 2, we begin by learning two two-dimensional ﬁeld theories that will be important for us: the two-dimensional q-deformed Yang-Mills theory and the Liouville theory.In Sec. 3, we introduce the class S theories of type SU(2), directly as four-dimensional ﬁeld theories deﬁned by Lagrangian associated to Riemann surfaces with decompositions to three-punctured spheres.

text: 2.2 The Liouville theory We will now study the second two-dimensional ﬁeld theory, known as the Liouville theory.It is the prime example of so-called irrational conformal ﬁeld theory.Here we cover only extremely shallow aspects of this beautiful and rich theory.An interested reader is referred to the classic reviews such as [14,15].We will mainly use a more axiomatic approach, pioneered and reviewed in [16].Before getting there, let us quickly recall the free boson theory. 2.2.1 Free boson theory A massless boson φ in two dimensions in the Euclidean signature satisﬁes the equation of motion △φ = ¯∂∂φ = 0.(2.31) A general solution is then φ(z, ¯z) = f(z) + ¯f(¯z) (2.32) where f(z) is a holomorphic function.From this we see that the classical theory has a symmetry under arbitrary holomorphic changes of the coordinate z 7→g(z).

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Denote the generator of the inﬁnitesimal transformation z →z(1 + ϵzn) by Ln.Classically they satisfy the commutation relation [Lm, Ln] = (m − n)Lm+n.In the quantum theory, the basic operator product expansion of the free boson theory is ∂φ(z)∂φ(w) ∼− 2(z −w)2 (2.33) and e2iaφ(z,¯z)e−2iaφ(w, ¯w) ∼ |z −w|2a2 .(2.34) The generator L0 rescales the coordinate as z 7→e−ϵL0z.Correspondingly, when the two- point function behaves as (z−w)−2∆(¯z−¯w)−2 ¯∆, we say that the operator has the holomorphic dimension L0 = ∆and the anti-holomorphic dimension ¯L0 = ¯∆.We ﬁnd ∂φ has (L0, ¯L0) = (1, 0) and e2iaφ has (L0, ¯L0) = (a2, a2).Quantum mechanically, the algebra generated by Ln is modiﬁed to [Lm, Ln] = (m −n)Lm+n + cm3 −m δm,−n (2.35) where c is a number called the central charge.This is the celebrated Virasoro algebra.

text: In a free-boson theory, the energy-momentum tensor T(z) is given by T(z) = (1/2)∂φ∂φ.A short computation reveals that it satisﬁes the relation (2.36) with c = 1.We now consider a slightly modiﬁed free-boson theory where the energy momentum tensor is given by T(z) = ∂φ∂φ + iQ∂2φ.(2.37) We ﬁnd that this satisﬁes the relation (2.36) with c = 1 + 6Q2.(2.38) This modiﬁcation corresponds to having the Lagrangian density L = gij∂iφ∂jφ + QφR (2.39) where R is the curvature of the 2d surface.When computing the correlators on the sphere, we can map it to a ﬂat inﬁnite plane, with the caveat that there is still a concentration of the curvature at z = ∞.This eﬀectively place an operator e−2Qφ at z = ∞.From this reason the parameter Q is often called the background charge.

text: This modiﬁes the basic correlator of the exponential ﬁelds (2.34) to e2(Q/2+ia)φ(z,¯z)e2(Q/2−ia)φ(w, ¯w) ∼ |z −w|2a2+Q2/2.(2.40) In particular, the exponential operator e2(Q/2+ia)φ has L0 = a2 + Q2/4.More generally, we say that the operator e2aφ has L0 = a(Q −a).(2.41) 2.2.2 Interacting theory Suppose now that we want to change this free boson theory with background charge Q into a full-ﬂedged interacting theory without destroying the conformal invariance.At leading order, a new term in the Lagrangian should have the dimension (L0, ¯L0) = (1, 1) to preserve the conformal invariance.From (2.41), we ﬁnd that the operator e2bφ does the job, when Q = b + 1 b.(2.42) Now the Lagrangian density is L = gij∂iφ∂jφ + QφR + 4πµe2bφ (2.43) where the parameter µ is often called the cosmological constant.

text: that the Lagrangian density (2.43) determines an interacting conformal ﬁeld theory with the central charge c = 1 + 6Q2 = 1 + 6(b + 1 b)2.(2.44) One crucial diﬀerence from the free theory is as follows.In the free theory, the operator e2ipφ with L0 = p2 gives rise to a state with momentum p moving the direction parameterized by φ, under the state-operator correspondence.In particular, two operators e2ipφ and e−2ipφ are two distinct states.Similarly, in the Liouville theory, the operator e(Q+2ip)φ with L0 = p2+(Q/2)2 corresponds to a state with momentum p in the φ-space.Here the shift of the exponent by Q is necessary to keep L0 real and positive.Due to the exponential interaction e2bφ, the wave coming from the negative φ region cannot penetrate to the positive φ region.Instead, it gets reﬂected by the exponential potential wall.

text: A class of four-dimensional theories In this section we introduce a class of four-dimensional N=2 supersymmetric gauge theories, commonly known as class S theories of type SU(2) in the literature.This class of theories was ﬁrst introduced in [4].For an extensive review, see e.g. [20].We start by quickly recalling the very basics of N=2 Lagrangians. 3.1 N=2 supersymmetric gauge theories We assume the reader knows the basics of N=1 superﬁelds.The N=2 theories we deal with can be obtained by imposing an SU(2)R symmetry that does not commute with the N=1 supersymmetry apparent in the N=1 formalism.Let us start with the N=2 vector multiplet.This consists of an N=1 vector multiplet V of a gauge group G, together with an N=1 chiral multiplet Φ in the adjoint representation of G.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: We consider the Lagrangian ℑτ 4π d4θ tr Φ†e[V,·]Φ + d2θ−i 8πτ tr WαW α + cc.(3.1) where τ = 4πi/g2 + θ/2π is the complexiﬁed gauge coupling.By expanding the superﬁelds into components, we see that the gaugino λ in V and the chiralino ψ in Φ have exactly the same couplings with the other ﬁelds, thus realizing SU(2)R symmetry.Next, we introduce the N=2 hypermultiplet, in the representation R of the gauge group G.This consists of a pair of N=1 chiral multiplets Q, ˜Q in the representation R and ¯R.The Lagrangian is d4θ(Q†eV Q + ˜Qe−V ˜Q†) + ( d2θ ˜QΦQ + cc.) (3.2) where µ is the mass term.Here, the SU(2)R symmetry rotates the scalar components of Q and ˜Q†.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The Lagrangian above describes a massless hypermultiplet.To give a mass term, we can give a vev to Φ in the Lagrangian above.For example, take a pair of hypermultiplets Qa i and ˜Qi a where a = 1, . . . , Nc and i = 1, . . . , Nf.This is in the bifundamental representation of SU(Nc) × U(Nf), and as such we have the coupling ˜Qi aΦa bQb i + ˜Qi aΦj iQa j (3.3) in the Lagrangian, where Φ is in the adjoint of SU(Nc) and Φ is in the adjoint of U(Nf).Now we regard Φ and its associated N=1 vector multiplet as external, background ﬁelds and just give a vev ⟨Φ⟩i j = mi j.We end up having a mass term of the form mi j ˜QiQj.To preserve SU(2)R invariance, we require [m, m†] = 0, which means that m is diagonalizable.It is known that this is the only way to give masses to hypermultiplets.When m = 0, the U(Nf) symmetry is a global ﬂavor symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: With generic nonzero diagonal m, this U(Nf) symmetry is further explicitly broken to U(1)Nf.We usually say that this mass term mi j ˜QiQj is associated to the ﬂavor symmetry U(Nf).We often abuse the terminology and say that the theory has the U(Nf) ﬂavor symmetry even when m̸ = 0.Finally let us introduce the half-hypermultiplet.When the representation R is pseudoreal, i.e. when R and ¯R are equivalent as representations and when there is a gauge-invariant antisymmetric two-form ϵab, we can impose the condition Qa = ϵab( ˜Q†)b (3.4) compatible with the SU(2)R invariance.This is called a half-hypermultiplet in the repre- sentation R.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Note that this consists of a single N=1 chiral multiplet in the representation R. 3.2 Class S theories of type SU(2) 3.2.1 Construction from three-punctured spheres and cylinders In Sec. 2, we recalled the properties of two two-dimensional ﬁeld theories.Very abstractly, two-dimensional ﬁeld theories associate complex numbers to two-dimensional surfaces.There, the essential point was to ﬁnd the amplitude associated to a three-punctured sphere or a three-holed sphere, and the amplitude associated to a cylinder.Here, we introduce a way to associate four-dimensional ﬁeld theories instead of complex numbers to two-dimensional surfaces.Again, the important point is to consider what to associate to a three-punctured sphere or a cylinder. i a u Q aiu Figure 7: A three punctured sphere corresponds to Qaiu, with SU(2)3 symmetry.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: First, take a three-punctured sphere, see Fig. 7.We associate an SU(2) ﬂavor symmetry for each of the three punctures.The fundamental representation of SU(2) is pseudoreal.Furthermore, the tensor product of an odd number of pseudoreal representations is pseudo- real.Therefore, the N=1 chiral multiplet in the representation (2, 2, 2) of SU(2)1 ×SU(2)2 × SU(2)3, which we denote as Qaiu, a = 1, 2;i = 1, 2;u = 1, 2 (3.5) forms a half-hypermultiplet.Here a, i, u are the indices for SU(2)1,2,3, respectively.Next, take a cylinder, see Fig. 8.We assign to it a complex number τ = 4πi/g2 + θ/2π, where g is real and θ ∼θ + 2π.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: We then associate to it an N=2 vector multiplet with gauge group SU(2), whose complexiﬁed coupling is τ. τ SU(2) vector multiplet with complexified coupling τ Figure 8: A cylinder with parameter τ corresponds to an SU(2) vector multiplet.Now, given a collection of three-punctured spheres, we pick two punctures.Let us say that the ﬁrst puncture is at z = 0 in a local coordinate z and the second is at w = 0 in a local coordinate w.We take a cylinder with parameter τ, and make the identiﬁcation zw = e2πiτ.(3.6) We also often use the notation q = e2πiτ.Correspondingly, we perform the following operation on the four-dimensional gauge the- ory side.By choosing two punctures, we picked up two SU(2) ﬂavor symmetries.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: We now couple them to a dynamical SU(2) gauge ﬁeld, whose complexiﬁed coupling constant is τ. 3.2.2 One-punctured torus Take one three-punctured sphere, and connect two punctures out of three, by a cylinder of parameter τ.The result is a torus of modulus τ with a puncture, see Fig. 9.As a gauge theory operation, we start from a trifundamental Qaiu.Pick the indices a and i, and we couple it to a single SU(2) gauge ﬁeld.We now regard two SU(2) symmetries acting on a and i as one and the same;as a doublet times a doublet is a triplet plus a singlet, we relabel Qaiu as AIu (I = 1, 2, 3) and Hu, where the index u = 1, 2 is still for an SU(2) ﬂavor symmetry.We end up with an N=2 SU(2) gauge theory with a triplet hypermultiplet formed by AI := AI,u=1, ˜AI := AI,u=2 and a decoupled hypermultiplet formed by H := Hu=1, ˜H := Hu=2.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: An N=2 gauge theory with gauge group G, together with a hypermultiplet in the adjoint representation of G, has an enhanced N=4 supersymmetry, and commonly known just as N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills.We can give a mass term using SU(2) ﬂavor

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: This has a nice interpretation in our geometric construction of gauge theories: we can con- struct a one-punctured torus with modular parameter τ in two ways from a three-punctured sphere and a cylinder, namely with a cylinder with parameter τ or with parameter −1/τ.Correspondingly, for this once-punctured torus, we have two gauge theories associated under our rule: N=4 theory with gauge group SU(2), with complexiﬁed gauge coupling τ or the same theory with gauge coupling −1/τ.The S-duality guarantees that these two theories are the same. 3.2.3 Four-punctured sphere Next, take two three-punctured spheres, and connect one puncture from a sphere and another puncture from another sphere, with a cylinder with parameter τ.This gives a four-punctured sphere.In the gauge theory language, we have two trifundamentals Qaiu and Q′ usx.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The indices a, i, s, x = 1, 2 are for four SU(2) symmetries, and we have a dynamical SU(2) gauge mul- tiplet acting on the index u = 1, 2.The one-loop beta function is zero.Again, the beta function is zero even non-perturbatively, and the complexiﬁed coupling constant is a genuine dimensionless parameter of the theory.We can reorganize the chiral matter ﬁelds into quI where u = 1, 2 and I = 1, . . . , 8.The superpotential coupling is δIJquIΦuvqvJ (3.7) where Φ is the adjoint chiral scalar of the SU(2) gauge multiplet.The indices uv are sym- metric, and therefore δIJ is symmetric too.This means that the ﬂavor symmetry is SO(8).This theory is often called SU(2) gauge theory with Nf = 4 ﬂavors.The four SU(2)s are

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: subgroups of this SO(8): SU(2)a × SU(2)i × SU(2)s × SU(2)x ⊂SO(8) (3.8) and the chiral matter ﬁelds transform as 2a ⊗2i ⊕2s ⊗2x = 8V (3.9) where 8V is the vector representation of the SO(8) ﬂavor symmetry. a i s x a s i x a x s i Figure 10: A four-punctured sphere can be decomposed in three diﬀerent ways.Now, a four-punctured sphere can be obtained in three distinct ways from two three- punctured spheres, see Fig. 10.We described one already.Two others also give SU(2) theories with Nf = 4 ﬂavors, but with diﬀerent SO(8) representation and with diﬀerent coupling constants.Namely, the matter ﬁelds in 2a ⊗2s ⊕2i ⊗2x = 8S (3.10) with coupling q′ = 1/q and the matter ﬁelds in 2a ⊗2x ⊕2s ⊗2i = 8C (3.11) with coupling q′′ = 1 −q.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Here, 8S and 8C are positive and negative chirality spinors of SO(8), and we used the exponentiated complexiﬁed coupling constants q = e2πiτ, q′ = e2πiτ ′, q′′ = e2πiτ ′′.Again, the S-duality guaranteeing the equivalence of these three descriptions has been known for quite some time. 3.2.4 General consideration Let us recapitulate what we have introduced so far.First, we gave a method to construct an N=2 gauge theory.The data was encoded in terms of the three-punctured spheres and cylinders connecting pairs of punctures.As can be easily checked, every gauge group corre- sponding to any cylinder has zero one-loop beta function.The N=2 supersymmetry then guarantees that all beta functions are zero even non-perturbatively, and therefore all gauge coupling constants remain genuine dimensionless parameters of the theory.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: The punctures that remain unused for connection via cylinders provide SU(2) ﬂavor symmetries.With k punctures we have SU(2)k ﬂavor symmetries, and if desired, we can turn on the correspond- ing k mass parameters.At this point, we have a Lagrangian ﬁeld theory for a given Riemann surface with punctures, with the decomposition into three-punctured spheres speciﬁed.Second, we considered a torus with one puncture can be constructed from two three- punctured spheres in two ways.The corresponding gauge theories were both N=4 super

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Yang-Mills with gauge group SU(2) with a decoupled hypermultiplet, but with diﬀerent coupling τ and −1/τ.They are known to be S-dual.Therefore, a torus with one puncture in fact corresponded to a single theory.Third, we considered a sphere with four-punctures.This can be constructed in three ways from two three-punctured spheres.The three corresponding gauge theories were SU(2) theories with Nf = 4 ﬂavors, but with hypermultiplets in distinct SO(8) ﬂavor representa- tions and with distinct coupling constants.Again, they are known to be S-dual.Therefore, a four-punctured sphere in fact corresponded to a single theory.In general, given a single Riemann surface with a number of punctures, there are multiple ways to cut it into three-punctured spheres and cylinders.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Each of such decompositions gives rise to a distinct Lagrangian of N=2 supersymmetric gauge theory.However, by combining the two S-dualities recalled above, any such decompositions can be related.Therefore, we conclude that a single Riemann surface with a number of punctures in fact corresponds to a single quantum ﬁeld theory, of which various distinct Lagrangians are just avatars.Two supersymmetric backgrounds In this section we ﬁrst discuss the general idea of supersymmetric localization, following the approach pioneered by [21] and reviewed in Contribution [22].We then discuss two explicit supersymmetric backgrounds, one based on S1 × S3 and another based on S4.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: More details on the former and the latter can be found in Contribution [23] and in Contribution [24], respectively. 4.1 General yoga of supersymmetric localization The energy-momentum tensor Tµν of a quantum ﬁeld theory describes how it couples to an external metric perturbation.Namely, let Z be the partition function as a functional of the metric.Then we have δ log Z = R δgµνT µνddx.By integrating this small variation, we know how a quantum ﬁeld theory behaves in a general curved manifold.In a supersymmetric theory, the energy-momentum tensor Tµν sits in a supermultiplet, containing the supercurrent Sµα and other components, depending on the dimension of the spacetime, the number of supersymmetries, and other subtler properties.In this review we are interested in N=2 theory in four dimensions.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: We then have the R-current JR µ and a scalar component X, both in the adjoint of SU(2)R.The energy-momentum tensor Tµν knows how the theory couples to the metric gµν.Sim- ilarly, the supercurrent Sµα knows how it couples to the gravitino background ψµα.The R-current JR µ knows how it couples to the R-symmetry background AR µ , and the scalar component X knows how it couples to the scalar background M.In short, the supermul- tiplet (Tµν, Sµα, JR µ , X, . . .) knows how it couples to the external supergravity background (gµν, ψµα, AR µ , M, . . .).There are many deﬁnitions of supermanifolds in the mathematical literature, but from the point of view of the supersymmetric ﬁeld theories, the most natu- ral super-version of a curved manifold is a manifold with the full supergravity background

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: speciﬁed.This point of view was emphasized ﬁrst in [21] and reviewed in more detail in Contribution [22].Similarly, if a theory has a global ﬂavor symmetry group G, it has a ﬂavor current Jµ, which knows how the theory couples to the ﬂavor symmetry background Aµ.When the theory is N=2 supersymmetric in four dimensions, Jµ sits in a supermultiplet containing a scalar operator K, that knows how to couple to a background scalar Φ, where both K and Φ are adjoint of G.In fact, the mass term of N=2 theory is just a special case of this construction, as we recalled in Sec. 3.1.Now, given a quantum ﬁeld theory on a curved manifold with isometry ξ, we have ⟨δξO⟩= 0 for any operator O.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Similarly, given a supersymmetric ﬁeld theory on a su- persymmetric background, i.e. a supergravity background with at least one superisometry ϵ, we have ⟨δϵO⟩= 0 for any operator O.It often happens that many natural bosonic operators in the Lagrangian can be written as δϵO.For example, suppose a coupling λ in the Lagrangian multiplies an operator X = δϵO.Then, the partition function is independent of λ, because ∂ ∂λ log Z = ⟨X⟩= ⟨δϵO⟩= 0.(4.1) Also, note that the superisometry variation of the supercurrent itself, δϵSµα, is given by a linear combination of the energy-momentum tensor and other bosonic components of the supermultiplet.This means that a certain variation of the metric can be combined with corresponding particular variations of R-symmetry and scalar backgrounds so that the par- tition function is independent of it.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: This makes the partition function on a supersymmetric background oblivious to detailed choice of the metric.Sometimes it depends only on the topology or the complex structure of the spacetime.When δ2 ϵ generates a bosonic isometry of the background, the partition function only depends on the topological property of that isometry, etc.It also often happens that we can choose a fermionic operator O such that δϵ 2O = 0, δϵO ≃ X ψ |δψ|2.(4.2) where ψ runs over the dynamical fermion ﬁelds in the theory.We then consider the defor- mation S →S(t) = S + t Z ddxδϵO.(4.3) Thanks to δϵ2O = 0, the deformed Lagrangian is still invariant under the superisometry ϵ.Then ∂ ∂t log Z(t) = Z ddx⟨δϵO⟩= 0 (4.4) for arbitrary t.In the large t limit, the integral localizes to the conﬁgurations satisfying δψ = 0 (4.5)

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: and ﬂuctuations around them.For this reason we often call δϵO as the localizing term.We parameterize the solutions to (4.5) by a space M = ⊔iMi where i is some label distinguishing the components.Then we have the equality Z = X i Z Mi ZclassicalZquadr. ﬂuct., (4.6) where Zclassical is the exponential of the classical action evaluated at a conﬁguration satis- fying (4.5), and Zquadr. ﬂuct. is the result of the Gaussian integrals of bosonic and fermionic ﬂuctuations.The interaction terms do not contribute in the t →∞limit.Often, each of the components Mi is ﬁnite dimensional, and therefore the partition function Z is given as a sum of explicit multiple integrals.Evaluating it is still a formidable task, but is inﬁnitely simpler than the original inﬁnite-dimensional path integral expression.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Now, let us discuss two particular classes of supersymmetric backgrounds for four-dimensional N=2 theories, on which the localization has been worked out in detail.The ﬁrst is S1 × S3 and the second is S4.We do not discuss the detailed derivations of the facts mentioned below.Happily, all the details can be found in Contribution [23] for S1×S3 and in Contribution [24] for S4. 4.2 S1 × S3 First, we consider N=2 superconformal theory on S1 × S3.An N=2 superconformal theory has SU(2)R × U(1)R R-symmetry.A class of supersymmetric backgrounds, where the super- symmetric localization can be performed, is speciﬁed by the ratio β of the radii of S1 and S3, and two holonomies of SU(2)R and U(1)R around S1.In total there are three parameters, commonly denoted by (p, q, t).

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Note that this q is independent of the exponentiated com- plexiﬁed coupling, also often denoted by q and is equal to e2πiτ.In fact, the vector multiplet Lagrangian is of the form ∼τδϵO, and therefore the partition function on this background is independent of the complexiﬁed gauge coupling τ.For brevity of the exposition, we only use the one-dimensional slice where p = 0, q = t.In this case q = e−β.When the N=2 theory in question has a ﬂavor symmetry G, we can choose an element g ∈G such that there is a background G gauge ﬁeld around S1 given by g.Then the partition function on this background is just a function of q = e−β and g ∈G.By considering the S1 direction as the time direction, the partition function can be written as Z(q, g) = trH(−1)Fq∆−Rg.

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: (4.7) Here, H is the Hilbert space of the superconformal theory on S3, which is equivalent to the space of point-like operators of the conformal theory on the ﬂat space, via the state- operator correspondence. ∆is then the scaling dimension of the operator, and R is the third component of the SU(2)R charge.From this structure this partition function is often called the superconformal index.For four-dimensional quantum ﬁeld theories, this concept was introduced in [7,8].

file: 08_source_code/SY03-07_2d_4d 对应关系简述/工程文件/work/full.txt
text: Correspondingly, the computation of Z(q, g) for an N=2 Lagrangian ﬁeld theory can be done either by counting the operators on a ﬂat space, or by performing the path integral on S1 × S3.In most of th literature it is done using the operator approach;for a through discussion for N=2 case, see [9].For a path-integral approach for N=4, see [25].Either way, we ﬁnd the following results.We ﬁrst represent the holonomy g ∈G around S1 using complex numbers in the form g = (z1, . . . , zr) ∈U(1)r ⊂G (4.8) where r is the rank of G.We can have an arbitrary ﬂavor holonomy.The gauge holonomy parameterizes the BPS conﬁgurations over which we integrate.
